entities.summary:
Gevherhan Hatun (d. 1514), an Ottoman imperial princess, served as a crucial dynastic link in the intricate diplomatic and political strategies of the Ottoman Empire during the late 15th and early 16th centuries. As the daughter of Sultan Mehmed II "the Conqueror" and Gülbahar Hatun, and the full-sister of Sultan Bayezid II, her marriages were instrumental in solidifying alliances and managing regional rivalries, particularly with the powerful Aq Qoyunlu confederation.

Her first marriage, arranged by her father Mehmed II around 1474, was to Uğurlu Mehmed Bey, son of Uzun Hasan, the formidable ruler of the Aq Qoyunlu Turkoman confederation. This union aimed to neutralize a persistent eastern threat and consolidate Ottoman influence in Anatolia. After Uğurlu Mehmed Bey's death in 1477, Gevherhan Hatun returned to Istanbul. She later married Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha, a distinguished statesman who served multiple terms as Grand Vizier under her brother Bayezid II and her nephew Selim I. Through these unions, she bore several children, extending the dynastic reach and influence of the Ottoman imperial house.

Through her strategic marriages, Gevherhan Hatun contributed to the stability and expansion of the Ottoman realm, embodying the practice of dynastic diplomacy that characterized imperial foreign policy. Her connections provided a crucial bridge between the Ottoman court and significant regional powers, helping to manage complex geopolitical landscapes. The children born from these unions further intertwined the destinies of the Ottoman dynasty with powerful Anatolian and Mamluk-era families.

Her life, spanning the reigns of two powerful sultans, illustrates the often-overlooked yet profound political agency exercised by royal women within the Ottoman system, whose personal histories were inextricably linked to the grand narrative of empire-building and consolidation.
